EXCLUSIVE IMPLIED EASEMENTS OVER AN ENCROACHING DRIVEWAY OR WALL (CIV. CODE §§ 806, 1069, 1104; CODE CIV. PROC. § 325; ROMERO V. SHIH; HIRSHFIELD V. SCHWARTZ; SHOEN V. ZACARIAS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 643 and 651 West Alegria Avenue · Los Angeles

WHAT THIS SHEET COVERS
This sheet collects what California law says about easements that arise by implication from a land transaction, and in particular about implied easements whose scope is broad enough that the owner of the burdened land is left with no practical use of the surface of the burdened strip. It is organized around Romero v. Shih (2024) 15 Cal.5th 680, in which the California Supreme Court held that such easements are not forbidden as a matter of law, together with the statutes that decision construes - Civil Code sections 806, 1069 and 1104 and Code of Civil Procedure section 325 - and the equitable easement decisions the trial court in that case relied on in the alternative.

The sheet is a record of statutory text and of what identified opinions hold and say. It states no conclusion about any particular strip of land, boundary, driveway, wall or deed, and it makes no prediction about how any court would rule on any set of facts. Where a court expressly declined to decide something, or where no decision was found on a point, the clause records that rather than filling the space.

Prepared for reference concerning 643 and 651 West Alegria Avenue in Los Angeles County, California, by Jordan Lee on September 13, 2026. The parcel labels the easterly parcel and the westerly parcel are used below only where a clause needs to distinguish the two sides of a shared boundary; they carry no legal conclusion about which parcel is which.

HOW CALIFORNIA LAW DISTINGUISHES AN EASEMENT FROM AN ESTATE
Romero v. Shih opens its analysis by separating the two kinds of interest in land that the rest of the doctrine depends on. Quoting Hansen v. Sandridge Partners, L.P. (2018) 22 Cal.App.5th 1020, the court described estates as ownership interests that are or may become possessory, and quoting Mehdizadeh v. Mincer (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 1296, it described an easement as a nonpossessory and restricted right that must be less than the right of ownership.

The measure of how far an easement reaches is statutory. Civil Code section 806, enacted in 1872 and unamended since, states the rule for every servitude on land, whether the servitude was created by grant or acquired by use. Romero treats that section as the overarching instruction that governs the scope question in implied easement cases as well as express ones.

The opinion also records, without deciding the point, the treatise position that a deed purporting to convey land the grantor does not own is a "wild deed" outside the chain of title. In the case before the court, several grant deeds for the benefited parcel had described the disputed eight-foot strip even though an approved lot line adjustment had never been completed, so the grantors did not own it.

THE IMPLIED EASEMENT STATUTE: CIVIL CODE SECTION 1104
California has a statute on implied easements. Civil Code section 1104 has stood unchanged since its enactment in 1872, and Romero v. Shih quotes it in full and describes it as the codification of the doctrine.

The statute operates on a transfer. Where a grantor conveys part of an estate without expressly granting an easement in the instrument, the section attaches to the conveyed part an easement to use the grantor's remaining land in the same manner and to the same extent as that land was "obviously and permanently used" for the benefit of the conveyed part when the transfer was agreed upon or completed. Romero restates that operation in its own words.

Section 1104 does not stand alone. Romero quotes the Supreme Court's earlier decision in Fristoe v. Drapeau (1950) 35 Cal.2d 5 for the proposition that section 1104 must be read together with section 806 and in the light of the common law rules on easements by implication, and the opinion states that the case law of implied easements is broader than section 1104 read in isolation would suggest - for instance, in recognizing easements by implied reservation although the statute speaks only of a grantee.

THE ELEMENTS COURTS STATE FOR AN IMPLIED EASEMENT
Romero v. Shih sets out the elements California appellate courts have distilled from the statute and the common law, quoting Thorstrom v. Thorstrom (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1406. The formulation has three parts: first, that the owner of property conveys or transfers a portion of it to another; second, that the owner's prior existing use was of a nature that the parties must have intended or believed the use would continue, meaning the existing use was either known to both or so obviously and apparently permanent that they should have known of it; and third, that the easement is reasonably necessary to the use and benefit of the quasi-dominant tenement.

The vocabulary is part of the doctrine. Romero explains that the portion being used is called the quasi-servient tenement and the portion benefited the quasi-dominant tenement, and that where the statutory conditions are otherwise satisfied a conveyance of the quasi-dominant tenement carries an implied easement over the quasi-servient tenement retained by the owner-grantor.

Under this formulation the operative moment is the division of title, not the later history of the parcels. Romero describes the plaintiff's burden as alleging and proving a specific set of circumstances surrounding a particular land transaction.

IMPLIED EASEMENTS ARE NOT FAVORED, AND THE EVIDENCE MUST BE CLEAR
Romero v. Shih states twice, in different parts of the opinion, that implied easements are not favored in the law, and it gives the reason: an implied easement deprives the owner of exclusive use, so courts do not lightly infer that the parties intended one.

The opinion attaches two further points to that caution. The first is a direction of construction drawn from Civil Code section 1069: because a reservation in a grant is construed against the grantor, a court will imply an easement in favor of a grantee more readily than in favor of a grantor. The second is the standard of proof. Romero describes the requirement as "clear evidence" of the parties' intent, taken with the circumstances attending the transaction, the situation of the parties, and the state of the thing granted.

The court returns to the same standard when it explains why it does not need to add an express-writing requirement: the common law, it says, already requires claimants to clear a high bar, because the preexisting use must have been so obviously and apparently permanent that the law may conclude the parties must have intended or believed the use would continue.

WHAT "EXCLUSIVE" MEANS WHEN APPLIED TO AN EASEMENT
Much of the disagreement in Romero v. Shih turned on the word "exclusive," and the Supreme Court stopped to define it. Drawing on the Restatement Third of Property, Servitudes, the opinion explains that exclusivity in the law of servitudes refers to the right to exclude others, that it is a matter of degree rather than a binary attribute, and that it has two aspects: who may be excluded, and the uses or area from which they may be excluded.

At one end of the range an easement holder may be confined to narrow uses with no right to exclude anyone who does not unreasonably interfere; at the other, the holder may have the right to exclude everyone, including the owner of the burdened land, from any use within the easement boundaries. Romero coins the terms "highly exclusive" and "broadly exclusive" for the second end of that range, and says that is what the Court of Appeal had meant.

Even at that end, the opinion says, the interest remains nonpossessory so long as the transferor is not excluded from the entire parcel and keeps the right to make uses that do not interfere.

THE HOLDING: AN IMPLIED EASEMENT MAY BE BROADLY EXCLUSIVE
The question the California Supreme Court took up in Romero v. Shih was whether the law forbids recognition of an implied easement that would effectively exclude the owners of the burdened land from most practical uses of the easement area. The Court of Appeal had held that it does. The Supreme Court held that it does not.

The court paired that holding with a caution about proof, stating that the evidentiary standard for an implied easement is a high one and will naturally be harder to meet as the easement approaches that degree of exclusivity.

The reasoning rests on scope being a question of intent. Romero states that the burden imposed on the servient tenement is measured by the parties' intent even where that intent was to create a privilege that effectively precludes the owners from their own use of the area, and that nothing in the language of the statutes imposes a requirement that some quantum of practical use be preserved for the owner. The opinion frames the result as confined to unusual cases.

WHY THE RULE AGAINST EXCLUSIVE PRESCRIPTIVE EASEMENTS DID NOT CARRY OVER
The Court of Appeal in Romero had reasoned from a line of prescriptive easement cases beginning with Raab v. Casper (1975) 51 Cal.App.3d 866 and running through Silacci v. Abramson (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 558, Mehdizadeh v. Mincer (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 1296, Harrison v. Welch (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 1084 and Hansen v. Sandridge Partners, L.P. (2018) 22 Cal.App.5th 1020. Those cases refuse a prescriptive easement that would leave the record owner with no practical use of the burdened land, on the ground that it would let a claimant take the fruits of adverse possession without meeting the adverse possession requirements.

The Supreme Court identified the concern as specific to prescription. Adverse possession and prescriptive easement are acquired the same way, by the claimant's own unilateral use, and their elements closely resemble each other - except that adverse possession requires proof of payment of taxes under Code of Civil Procedure section 325, subdivision (b), and prescription does not. Romero quotes Hansen for the proposition that maintaining the distinction is especially important in the prescription context because otherwise the tax requirement would be nullified.

An implied easement, the court held, raises none of that. Proving one requires proving the circumstances of a particular land transaction, which bears little resemblance to the elements of adverse possession. On that ground the court declined to extend the Raab line.

THE ALTERNATIVE ROUTE: EQUITABLE EASEMENTS AND THE RELATIVE HARDSHIP DOCTRINE
The trial court in Romero created an equitable easement in the alternative, to take effect if the implied easement were overturned, and conditioned it on payment of damages. The Supreme Court described that body of law without disturbing it, and the Court of Appeal had affirmed the equitable easement and its $69,000 award.

The doctrine is older than the label. Hirshfield v. Schwartz traces it to Christensen v. Tucker (1952) 114 Cal.App.2d 554 and describes the operation as an equitable balancing, undertaken after a trespass is established, between enjoining the trespass and awarding damages instead. Hirshfield states that the burden starts against the encroacher: doubtful cases are decided for the plaintiff.

Three factors must be present before an injunction may be denied. The encroacher must be innocent, meaning the encroachment was neither willful nor negligent; the injunction should issue if the plaintiff would suffer irreparable injury, unless public rights would be harmed; and the hardship to the encroacher from an injunction must be greatly disproportionate to the hardship the encroachment causes the plaintiff, a fact that must clearly appear in the evidence and be proved by the encroacher. Shoen v. Zacarias states the same three prerequisites and adds that unless all three are established a court lacks discretion to grant the easement at all.

THE LIMITS COURTS PLACE ON EQUITABLE EASEMENTS
Shoen v. Zacarias is largely an account of what the equitable easement doctrine is not. The court reviewed a trial court that had granted an easement on its own view of "whatever it deems important," and held that the equitable character of the doctrine confers no such license when the three prerequisites are absent. Review is for abuse of discretion.

Shoen also warns that the familiar labels mislead. Calling the doctrine a balancing of conveniences or of relative hardships suggests that an easement may issue whenever the hardships merely favor the trespasser, and suggests the parties begin in equipoise; the court says the doctrine requires disproportion, and says the hardships begin tipped toward the owner because of the owner's interest in exclusive use arising from ownership itself.

Two reasons are given. The first is that the doctrine was crafted to stop an owner inconvenienced to a minor degree from practicing what the cases call legal extortion against an innocent trespasser. The second is that an equitable easement gives the trespasser what amounts to a private right of eminent domain, which is in tension with the constitutional prohibition on takings - which is why, Shoen says, courts approach these easements with an abundance of caution and resolve doubts against issuing them.

Hirshfield adds a separate limit from the other direction: it holds that the prescriptive easement cases are not the source of the constraint, because those decisions were concerned solely with defending the integrity of the adverse possession laws, and that equity is a different matter whose principal concern is to promote justice.

THE CONSTITUTIONAL ARGUMENT, AND WHAT THE COURT ACTUALLY ORDERED
The owners of the burdened parcel in Romero argued that recognizing an exclusive implied easement violated the Due Process and Takings Clauses of the Fifth Amendment. The court held the point forfeited because it had not been raised below, and then rejected it on the merits in the alternative.

The reasoning was that an implied easement finding creates no new property right. It clarifies rights already fixed by the intentions of the parties when the parcels were severed, which means the later purchasers took subject to the easement and their bundle of rights never included the use in question. The court cited the plurality opinion in Stop the Beach Renourishment, Inc. v. Florida Dept. of Environmental Protection (2010) 560 U.S. 702 for the proposition that courts clarifying previously unclear entitlements have not taken an established property right.

The disposition was narrow. The court reversed the Court of Appeal on the implied easement cause of action and remanded, framing the question on remand as whether the evidence shows the parties clearly intended the preexisting use of the quasi-servient tenement to continue after separation of title. It added that evidence of an intent to effectuate a variance or lot line adjustment does not, considered in the abstract, eliminate the possibility of such an intent, and expressed no view on the weight of that evidence in the case.

California has a statute on implied easements. Civil Code section 1104 has stood unchanged since its enactment in 1872, and Romero v. Shih quotes it in full and describes it as the codification of the doctrine.

The statute operates on a transfer. Shoen v. Zacarias is largely an account of what the equitable easement doctrine is not. The court reviewed a trial court that had granted an easement on its own view of "whatever it deems important," and held that the equitable character of the doctrine confers no such license when the three prerequisites are absent. Review is for abuse of discretion.

Shoen also warns that the familiar labels mislead. Calling the doctrine a balancing of conveniences or of relative hardships suggests that an easement may issue whenever the hardships merely favor the trespasser, and suggests the parties begin in equipoise; the court says the doctrine requires disproportion, and says the hardships begin tipped toward the owner because of the owner's interest in exclusive use arising from ownership itself.

Two reasons are given. The first is that the doctrine was crafted to stop an owner inconvenienced to a minor degree from practicing what the cases call legal extortion against an innocent trespasser. The second is that an equitable easement gives the trespasser what amounts to a private right of eminent domain, which is in tension with the constitutional prohibition on takings - which is why, Shoen says, courts approach these easements with an abundance of caution and resolve doubts against issuing them.

Hirshfield adds a separate limit from the other direction: it holds that the prescriptive easement cases are not the source of the constraint, because those decisions were concerned solely with defending the integrity of the adverse possession laws, and that equity is a different matter whose principal concern is to promote justice.

citations.quote: Contrary to the trial court’s suggestion, the equitable nature of this doctrine does not give a court license to grant easements on the basis of “whatever [a court] deems important,” even when these prerequisites are absent.
We review the trial court’s application of this doctrine for an abuse of discretion.

These labels suggest that an equitable easement may issue if the conveniences or hardships merely favor the trespasser, when the doctrine actually requires that they tip disproportionately in favor of the trespasser.

These labels also suggest that the conveniences or hardships between the trespasser and property owner start out in equipoise, when the doctrine actually requires that they begin tipped in favor of the property owner due to the owner’s substantial interest in exclusive use of her property arising solely from her ownership of her land.

citations.quote: First and most fundamentally, courts first crafted equitable easements to prevent a property owner inconvenienced to a “minor degree” by a trespass from nevertheless engaging in “legal extortion” against an innocent trespasser by demanding an exorbitant sum in exchange for not filing suit to enjoin the trespass.

citations.case: Shoen v. Zacarias (quoting Christensen v. Tucker)
citations.quote: Second, equitable easements give the trespasser “what is, in effect, the right of eminent domain by permitting him to occupy property owned by another.”

Instead, by prohibiting a prescriptive easement, which amounts to an unauthorized award of adverse possession, Raab, Silacci and Mehdizadeh concerned themselves solely with defending the integrity of the adverse possession laws.
When a court exercises its equity powers, its principal concern is to promote justice, acting through its conscience and good faith.

The reasoning was that an implied easement finding creates no new property right. It clarifies rights already fixed by the intentions of the parties when the parcels were severed, which means the later purchasers took subject to the easement and their bundle of rights never included the use in question. The court reversed the Court of Appeal on the implied easement cause of action and remanded, framing the question on remand as whether the evidence shows the parties clearly intended the preexisting use of the quasi-servient tenement to continue after separation of title. It added that evidence of an intent to effectuate a variance or lot line adjustment does not, considered in the abstract, eliminate the possibility of such an intent, and expressed no view on the weight of that evidence in the case.
